title: BBC upholds complaints over Victoria Beckham slur on Have I Got News For You
description: Complaints about the broadcast of a swear word in connection with Victoria Beckham during an episode of BBC One's Have I Got News For You have been up
body: Complaints about the broadcast of a swear word in connection with Victoria Beckham during an episode of BBC One's Have I Got News For You have been upheld, the corporation's executive complaints unit (ECU) has ruled.The show, from 7 November last year, hosted by comic and presenter Katherine Ryan, featured an email allegedly sent by Sir David Beckham in which the word was used.Ryan told the show's panellists: "I don't know that we are allowed to broadcast the c-word, but you did reference Victoria Beckham earlier and we'll allow that."Two viewers complained that this was gratuitously offensive, and the BBC said there was no justification for a comment which "presented Victoria Beckham as equivalent to a particularly offensive word". The ECU finding has been reported to the management of BBC Content.As a result, a version of the programme edited in light of the finding will replace the version currently on iPlayer.The ECU statement in full said: "The relevant BBC Editorial Guidelines do not require programmes to avoid giving offence, but do require that any offence should be editorially justified."In the ECU's judgement, while the inclusion of the c-word in the programme derived editorial justification from David Beckham's alleged use of it and the satirical reflections this prompted, there was no such justification for a comment which presented Victoria Beckham as equivalent to a particularly offensive word."In November, the ECU responded to complaints from viewers it said were "unhappy with the inclusion of strong language in the programme".It said "the use of the strong language was editorially justified as the panel were discussing a current news story about Sir David Beckham and directly quoting from leaked emails in which he had used the word in question, leading to further discussion".It added that it was "common practice" to carry a clear verbal warning at the start of post-watershed programmes with very strong language, which was what happened for this particular episode of the show. "It is never our intention to offend our audience," the statement added.

schema.headline: BBC upholds complaints over Victoria Beckham slur on Have I Got News For You

title: Shooting outside Canadian synagogue was 'hate-motivated', officials say
description: Canadian authorities have confirmed a shooting near a synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, was a "hate-motivated" attack targeting the Jewish community.
body: Canadian authorities have confirmed a shooting near a synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, was a "hate-motivated" attack targeting the Jewish community. The shooting took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday night during Yom Kippur, the holiest night in the Jewish calendar.Belleville police chief Murray Rodd said during a Thursday news conference that it was "a deliberate attack directed at members of the Jewish community".A police officer who was critically injured in the incident continued to fend off the attacker despite being shot multiple times, the police chief said.The officer, identified as Constable Jeff Smith, suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his head and body, Rodd said. Smith remains in hospital and is expected to undergo multiple surgeries related to "serious head trauma"."He's making progress every day," the chief said.Smith was shot in his car but sought to fend off the attack on the synagogue until a second officer arrived almost three minutes later."Despite suffering life-threatening injuries, within moments of encountering the armed suspect, Constable Smith exited his vehicle and engaged the attacker," Rodd said.The second officer, Constable Mike McCurdy, "joined the active gunfight, helping to bring the violent attack to an end", the police chief said. McCrudy was not injured.Both officers discharged their firearms, authorities said earlier this week. Around 20 to 30 shots were fired, leaving the suspect in life-threatening condition and Smith in critical but stable condition.The gunman was identified by police as 29-year-old Sean Ward from Quinte West, a community near Belleville and about 170km (105 miles) east of Toronto. He was sent to hospital with serious injuries and later died.Rodd called the attempted attack a "hate-motivated crime".Toronto police have increased patrols outside synagogues and places of worship out of an abundance of caution.Leaders of the Jewish community, as well as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and other politicians, condemned antisemitic violence in the aftermath of the incident.Noah Shack, CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, said in a statement on Thursday that "if not for the extraordinary bravery of Constable Jeff Smith, Canadians would have experienced the type of mass-casualty terror attack our security services have warned is a realistic possibility". He called on Canadian leaders to "take urgent and concrete actions" against threats toward the Jewish community. Carney wrote on X earlier this week that "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives."

schema.headline: Shooting outside Canadian synagogue was 'hate-motivated', officials say

title: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
description: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any
body: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class. A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school.Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year.Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality."You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition.There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear.The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible. The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf.The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through.Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU.The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently.In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school. In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system.Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching. The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained.The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered.The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law.The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools. Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank.The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren.Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge. "We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said.Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago. The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government".Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals.

schema.headline: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Jos Buttler's bravery in vain as tourists fight back to level series
description: Second Metro Bank one-day international, Headingley Sri Lanka 321-6 (50 overs): Kusal 121, Kamindu 54; Ahmed 2-48England 305-9 (50 overs): Banton 73,
body: Second Metro Bank one-day international, Headingley Sri Lanka 321-6 (50 overs): Kusal 121, Kamindu 54; Ahmed 2-48England 305-9 (50 overs): Banton 73, Buttler 69; Wellalage 3-49Sri Lanka won by 16 runs ScorecardJos Buttler's bravery came in vain as Sri Lanka fought back to beat England in the second one-day international at Headingley and set up a series decider at The Oval.Needing 68 from 75 balls, England were cruising towards a target of 322 until Buttler retired hurt on 67 after tweaking a hamstring.When Rehan Ahmed, Gus Atkinson and Jamie Overton fell, Buttler re-emerged with 27 needed from 14 balls and witnessed Will Jacks fall for 52 at the non-striker's end.England were left needing 19 from the last with Buttler on strike but, barely able to hobble a single, he holed out at deep mid-wicket. England finished on 306-9 as Sri Lanka won by 16 runs.Buttler had earlier shown flashes of his vintage best in hitting Sri Lanka's spinners for five sixes, putting England on course after collapse of 3-14 spoiled an opening stand of 143 between Tom Banton and Ben Duckett.Sri Lanka were fortunate for the way he was abruptly halted but deserve credit for the way their seamers used reverse swing afterwards to deny England's lower order.Their captain Kusal Mendis also hit a fine 122 in their 321-6. The series, and the international summer, concludes on Sunday from 10:30 BST.What to make of this dramatic encounter? It is a defeat for England, one which halts their momentum a touch as they build towards next year's 50-over World Cup.It was unlike any other, however. They will do well to find situations like these again when the bigger moments come."It is always disappointing when you lose," captain Harry Brook said. "Sri Lanka played exceptionally well there, especially the last 10-15 overs. There were plenty of moments in the game we could have been slightly better."One positive was the batting of Buttler before injury struck. He has not scored a century in this format for three-and-a-half years and had his T20 form doubted earlier this year at the World Cup.The way he took down the spinners was brutal. When he was flying, England were on course for their highest chase at this ground. The opening stand between Banton and Duckett was also impressive - reminiscent of England's brightest ODIs days as they thrashed around the bowling at more than seven runs an over.That neither pressed on - Duckett was bowled for 67 and Banton stumped for 73, both to left-arm spinner Dinuth Wellalage - was disappointing. There were also rare failures for Joe Root who made 15 and Brook, the latter also pinned in front lbw for one by Wellalage.Perhaps more concerning was that the lower order were unable to support Jacks in his quest to push England over the line again. That aspect must improve over England's three white-ball series that come before mid-January.This has been a difficult tour for Sri Lanka, who were outclassed in the 3-0 T20 series defeat and well beaten by 89 runs in the first ODI at Chester-le-Street.This, especially given the bad start with the ball, will be a significant boost to morale.Kusal was troubled early on by Overton's bouncers, top-edging one into a gap soon after Atkinson dropped a simple chance at fine leg when the right-hander had 17 - another England error. The Sri Lanka captain also had to overturn a caught-behind decision on 99 when Overton was the bowler again.Kusal was eventually caught on the boundary trying to clear deep mid-wicket off Ahmed, who also had Charith Asalanka caught in the same position for 2-48 but did not offer the control usually brought by Adil Rashid.A flat Headingley pitch was a far bigger test of England's seamers than Tuesday's difficult surface in Durham.Josh Tongue struggled with his lines for 0-50 in seven overs. Atkinson, who took 2-55, and Overton, who had another catch dropped in the final over, in taking 0-63 from 10 were England's best bowling performers."Tight games are always good games to watch and good games to be a part of," Brook added."Having the opportunity to play in a decider will only benefit us."

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Jos Buttler's bravery in vain as tourists fight back to level series

title: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
description: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war c
body: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region. Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

schema.headline: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany

title: Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far
description: At least so far, Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has been all pomp and little obvious progress on pressing issues.From the ceremoni
body: At least so far, Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has been all pomp and little obvious progress on pressing issues.From the ceremonial welcoming at a military air base on Wednesday to the honour-guard arrival at the White House this morning, President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet – literally and figuratively – for his Chinese counterpart.The public remarks from the two leaders have teemed with warm words and diplomatic niceties. In a statement before today's formal meetings, Xi announced a gift of Chinese pandas and unveiled a new student exchange programme."Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world," he said.Trump, for his part, outlined some of the topics the leaders planned to discuss in their meetings, including "pressing issues concerning security, technology, and superintelligence" - using his preferred term for artificial intelligence."The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," he said.The marching bands and military flyovers on Thursday may serve a larger purpose, however – at least for Trump."This is a little bit of intentional pageantry to talk up the positive vibes of the summit," Jennifer Welch, chief economic analyst for Bloomberg Economics, told the BBC. "This is very much how President Trump sees the summit and the role he plays in the US-China relationship, as ballast to provide stability."Even so, there is still an edge to some of Xi's rhetoric, she notes.In remarks at the White House, the Chinese leader again mentioned the "Thucydides trap" – a theory that shifts in global power tend to lead to conflict between rising and declining nations."China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust," Xi said.The obstacles in the way of reaching any substantive agreement between the two nations are significant, however. When Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, the men agreed to form boards of trade and investment to oversee economic interactions, and little more.On Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a year-long trade "truce" between the two nations that had kept tariffs lower would be extended another two months. Financial analysts expect a further extension could come before this week's summit ends, given that neither side wants a renewal of last year's trade war.The outlook for progress is much dimmer on other topics, like the US war with Iran, the Ukraine war and regulating AI. China's reneging on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to also sell more rare earth minerals to the US is helping cloud the outlook. China, meanwhile, is watching to see if Trump follows through on a proposed sale of American weapons to China, which has been on hold for months.When it comes to AI, China and the US have two very different goals for any agreement on the race to develop the technology, Robyn Klingler-Vida, a professor of political economy at Kings College London, told the BBC. "On the US side, it's about existential risk and slowing down AI potentially," she said. "Whereas in China, it's about acceleration, maybe winning the AI tech race and the application of AI to the real economy."A number of leading American AI executives plan to attend tonight's formal state dinner at the White House, which many view as a means for the US side to tout its current technological advantage.Muscle-flexing aside, more pageantry – and the promise of stability – may be the end result of Xi's China visit, even with additional face time between the two leaders to come before Xi departs on Friday afternoon."What China talks about is metaphysical and abstract. The United States wants to solve specific problems," Miles Yu, who served as principal China policy planner and strategist to Secretary of State Mike Pompeo during Trump's first term, told the BBC. "These different approaches are not going to lead to any result."

schema.headline: Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far

title: Fury vs Joshua: The compromises & power struggles that shaped heavyweight fight
description: After a decade of stalled negotiations, public squabbling and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in the ring on 11 December
body: After a decade of stalled negotiations, public squabbling and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in the ring on 11 December at Cardiff's Principality Stadium.BBC Sport understands the WBA 'Super' heavyweight title is expected to be on the line, although confirmation from the governing body is still awaited.It would give both former world champions the chance to regain a version of the heavyweight crown, although Fury-Joshua has always been about more than belts.The fight arrives later than anybody wanted, with both in the twilight of their careers, but for years British boxing's biggest heavyweight rivalry seemed destined to remain a story of what might have been.Yet Thursday's announcement of an 80,000-capacity showdown, broadcast globally by Netflix, did more than finally provide a date and venue.It also offered a glimpse of the competing interests, egos and power struggles involved in getting one of boxing's most elusive fights over the line.Speaking to BBC Sport after the fight was announced, Fury's promoter Frank Warren repeatedly returned to one word: compromise."Everybody's got to make a compromise," the Queensberry boss said. "Tyson really compromised. He didn't dig his heels in."He said, 'Fine, wherever they want it, I'll do it. If they want me to go to New York, I'll go. They want it in the UK, I just want to get the fight on."The fighters had already agreed to the contest but the venue was a sticking point.Warren says Netflix wanted New York, while Joshua, 36, was determined to fight in Britain. Predictably, their camps disagree over who finally got it done.Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn described the push to keep the fight in Britain as a "two-man crusade"."AJ has turned down money to keep it in the UK," Hearn told the Matchroom YouTube channel. "I wouldn't be able to look people in the eye if I was part of the movement to take this to the US."Hearn says Joshua had specifically requested protection for a UK fight in his contract and refused to relent."We were under so much pressure to fold," he added. "It was only really the support of the British public that made Joshua stand 10 toes down and say no."Warren sees it differently.He says Fury, 38, could have insisted on his own contractual position but instead accepted Britain to ensure the fight did not collapse.Perhaps the biggest sideshow has been the struggle for influence around the promotion itself.Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh announced the fight, having previously insisted any confirmation would come from him."For 15 years no-one has been able to make this fight," he wrote. "Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury v Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over."Dana White's involvement is particularly intriguing.The UFC chief is partnered with Alalshikh through Zuffa Boxing and featured prominently in the announcement, with Netflix describing the event as a collaboration involving White and Alalshikh's The Ring. Hearn and Warren were absent.Hearn had previously said White would not be involved in promoting the fight, while Warren says both fighters' contracts stipulated the same.Yet Warren says White ultimately helped secure the Netflix deal but believes fans care little about the promotional politics."I don't know whether he will be front and centre or not," Warren said.Wednesday's news conference in London may tell us more - not least how prominent White is and how he and Hearn share the stage after months of back-and-forth.

schema.headline: Fury vs Joshua: The compromises & power struggles that shaped heavyweight fight

title: Swansea woman's migraines dismissed by GP as 'dramatic'
description: Lauren, from Swansea, said: "Although the 'headache' is in the head it can affect body temperature, digestive system, speech, light sensitivity, limb
body: Lauren, from Swansea, said: "Although the 'headache' is in the head it can affect body temperature, digestive system, speech, light sensitivity, limb numbness, ability to walk and carry out a journey, brain fog, sleep, neck pain, mood swings, visual aura, sound sensitivity, cravings, vertigo."I would wake up daily either in pain or worried about when it would start."She also spent a huge amount of time researching triggers and spent "hundreds on various things just to see if that would help" - from vitamins to chiropractors.Lauren was training to become a biomedical scientist in the NHS but the lights and overstimulation of Singleton Hospital were so intense she had daily migraines. She added that she often felt dismissed by colleagues who implied she was faking her condition but was lucky that her manager was supportive.Some colleagues would accommodate her by turning off the lights, she said, but others said: "If you don't get your annual leave approved, you can just say you've got a migraine and you won't come in."She continued: "That was so untrue. So you're battling, not just your physical health, you're battling all the mental side that comes with it as well."If I went home every day at the sight of a migraine, I would never be in work. There wasn't a day without pain and if there was, I'd be waiting for it."To manage her symptoms, Lauren changed her working hours, starting at 08:00 BST and finishing at 16:00 so she could get home to take medication, but was still "in agony". "I couldn't make plans because I knew I'd be suffering in the evening. My weekends would basically be spent recovering," she said.Lauren saw a crisis team in December, was signed off work for a month and her migraine attacks began to ease.She decided it was time to leave her biomedical scientist career and now has a job at an insurance firm, and feels like a different person."I have never done so many hobbies in my life," she said."Jewellery making, painting... and running 50k in September for a charity."Her new medication is working well, but she added: "If it got bad again, I honestly wouldn't know where to turn to."Swansea Bay health board said it was "very sorry to hear of the patient's concerns" but could not comment on individual cases without consent and "would welcome the patient getting in touch with us so we can discuss this further". It said it had a "specialist headache clinic that covers conditions such as migraine, which GPs can refer people to when appropriate".Munro said headaches were a symptom of migraine attacks, but so were "visual disturbances, nausea and vomiting, sometimes numbness and tingling, sometimes abdominal pain, sometimes dizziness". They are also a spectrum condition, she said, from episodic - meaning people have mild or rare attacks - to chronic, where they have more than 15 days a month affected by migraine symptoms. "If you have a migraine attack and you put up with it and then you have another one and put up with it, your brain actually gets more irritable," she said.That means the migraines become more regular and can become chronic if effective treatment is not applied.The first barrier to treatment, Munro said, is that a lot of people believe they are "normal headaches".She said people should always get repetitive headaches checked out by a GP.The next barrier is that GPs often just note down the headaches as a symptom rather than diagnose migraine, while the third barrier is the medication that was offered in the past, though this has improved in the last five years, she said."We need better education throughout the whole of society about how significant migraine is to people who suffer from it."The Migraine Trust speaks to about 5,000 people with the condition each year through its support services and Rob Music, chief executive of the charity said: "We have seen a concerning trend in enquiries relating to decline in mental health and wellbeing.""When people are already struggling with the impact of migraine, being met with doubt that it really is 'that bad' by employers, healthcare professionals and even loved ones can be devastating," he said. The Welsh government said it recognised the effect migraines could have on people's lives and guidance was available to help NHS staff diagnose and manage conditions.The UK government said the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) had "clear guidance on the diagnosis and management of migraines, and we expect healthcare professionals to follow it and deliver high-quality care to all patients".If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Swansea woman's migraines dismissed by GP as 'dramatic'

title: County Durham breast cancer failure bosses to review 4,500 more cases
description: NHS trust to review 4,500 more breast cancer cases after failingsFigure caption, Watch: Denise (pictured), Pam and other women describe how they were
body: NHS trust to review 4,500 more breast cancer cases after failingsFigure caption, Watch: Denise (pictured), Pam and other women describe how they were failedByDuncan Leatherdale and Sharon BarbourNorth East and Cumbria health correspondentUpdated 9 hours agoHospital chiefs in County Durham have agreed to review up to a further 4,500 breast cancer cases after failings including delayed diagnoses and unnecessary surgeries were found.Hundreds of patients suffered harm under County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, according to a review of cases dating back to 2023.The BBC previously investigated the failings and has spoken to multiple women affected, including one who said she felt "mutilated" and the trust's mistakes were "absolutely unforgivable".Ahead of agreeing to expand the review to cases dating back to 2015, members of the trust's board offered "sincere" apologies for the failings and harm caused.At an extraordinary meeting of the board held in Durham, board chair Alison Marshall said: "I would like to offer a sincere apology to all the women and their families who have been affected by the failings in our breast services."I can't imagine the impact that has had."She said they could "not turn back the clock" but would be "open, honest and transparent" about the failings.Chief nurse Gill Hunt told the board concerns were first raised in 2015 after a "service reconfiguration" and loss of breast surgical trainee posts.Over the following years patients and bodies such as the Northern Cancer Alliance, Care Quality Commission and NHS England raised multiple issues, she said.The key "themes" included treatment "not aligned to best practice", excessive surgery and delayed diagnosis, she said.The trust's breast surgery lookback review began in April 2025 by examining cases between January 2023 and February 2025.Hunt said 538 cases had been reviewed so far with 321 having experienced some form of harm, including one death.Image source, CDDFTImage caption, The trust has been reviewing breast cancer care at its hospitals and services in County Durham and DarlingtonAbout 640 patients had also contacted a special helpline asking for their cases to be reviewed, the board heard.The review cost about £523,000 in its first year and involved nine reviewers looking at about 80 cases a month, the report said.The board agreed to extend the review by one year at a time back to 2015, which would encompass up to 4,500 further cases and take an estimated five years to complete.Hunt said the expanded review would "provide a proportionate and evidence-led clinical approach" in response to "emerging findings", while decisions would be "supported by clear clinical rationale and formal governance review".Other "important learning" to come out of the review so far was about how bosses should respond to concerns raised by patients or other agencies, Hunt said."We are committed to doing the right thing," she said. Breast Cancer Scandal: Exposing the HarmBBC health correspondent Sharon Barbour investigates a deepening breast cancer scandal in County Durham and hears from women whose mastectomies were unnecessary.Watch on BBC iPlayer nowChief executive Steve Russell said the trust was "incredibly conscious women and their families" had experienced "distress, uncertainty and harm".He said no apology could undo that but the trust would "support women who have been impacted" in any way possible.For example, some women who had undergone unnecessary mastectomies could be offered breast reconstruction surgery as they previously should have been, Russell said.He also said the trust was currently exceeding national standards for breast cancer treatment, including for the number of women having breast conservation surgeries and being offered immediate reconstruction."None of that changes what has happened to women in the past but hopefully gives confidence the changes made in the service have had an impact on the outcomes," Russell said.He said patients today could be "confident" they would be "treated appropriately" and get "good clinical outcomes".The helpline, which is available by phone or email, would remain open with any concerned patients encouraged to contact it "irrespective" of when they were treated, he said.Image caption, Denise was one of the women who had an unnecessary mastectomy  Denise Howarth attended the board meeting along with other patients.The 51-year-old from Consett, County Durham, who had an unnecessary mastectomy, said she was "pleased" the review would be extended as there could be many more cases still to be revealed.But past patients needed to be contacted with "dignity" and "compassion", she added, to try and reduce the "shock" and "pain" of being told their cases were being reviewed because of possible failings.She also said a public inquiry needed to be held and, as her case dated back to 2012, the trust's review should also look back further than 2015.Image caption, Rachel Gray contacted the trust's review helplineRachel Gray, 41 and from Sunderland, said she contacted the helpline after hearing of women "being harmed", with the review finding she could have avoided having a mastectomy at the age of 37.She said discovering that made her "want to crawl out of my skin".The board's decision to review more cases would mean there would be "more answers" and women finding out what had happened to them, she said.She also said she thought the review would find more women harmed "than what they are predicting".Medical negligence solicitor Chloe Gibson, who is representing women affected by the breast cancer scandal, said she welcomed the board's decision but warned the process would be "very long" and last until the 2030s.Waiting for their cases to be reviewed would cause "further anxiety and trauma" for many, she said, adding: "Justice delayed is justice denied."She also said the review should look further back than 2015 while a full public inquiry was the "only way proper scrutiny and full accountability can be achieved".Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external. Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? If you feel able to do so, please get in touch.

title: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
description: A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arr
body: A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław.Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil". Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way. Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds.The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released.Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident.Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law".Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances".The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack. In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law."Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

schema.headline: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey

title: Trump media ban: White House restores access to CNN, Politico and MS NOW after judge's order
description: CNN, Politico and MS NOW are back in the White House, hours after a federal judge ruled President Donald Trump's ban on the three news outlets was pro
body: CNN, Politico and MS NOW are back in the White House, hours after a federal judge ruled President Donald Trump's ban on the three news outlets was probably unconstitutional and ordered their access immediately restored.The outlets sought an emergency court hearing to regain entry accusing the White House in a court filing of having "repeatedly violated" the judge's ruling by turning away their journalists. The hearing was called off after access was restored. Trump initially said he barred the outlets because of "fake news". The White House later cited national security.But in his overnight ruling, Judge Timothy Kelly cast doubt on the claim about national security concerns.The chaotic standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House ahead of a state dinner later. Judge Kelly ruled the ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".CNN, Politico and MS Now all reported being denied entry to the White House on Thursday morning, prompting their request for an emergency hearing.In response, the director of White House Operations said in a court filing that the press passes and confiscated badges had been restored by 09:45. Shortly afterwards, all three outlets said they were allowed back in.However, networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC, which pulled out in solidarity, have yet to confirm they will resume broadcast coverage from the White House.

schema.headline: Trump media ban: White House restores access to CNN, Politico and MS NOW after judge's order

title: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-easte
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026ByNardine SaadUpdated 4 hours agoRapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made  onstage earlier this month."So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday. The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself.In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now"."What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention." Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done."Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October. US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week.Figure caption, "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at showWhile performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University.After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group. His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well. Sheeran addressed the controversy head-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week. He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

schema.headline: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout

title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas charged after dinghy slashed in Channel
description: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the English Chann
body: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the English Channel.The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, has also been charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone, Hampshire Police said.He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court via videolink on Friday, the force added.Several hundred people had gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening believing Thomas was inside.The demonstration, which seemed to pass off peacefully, began shortly before 18:30 BST. Protesters stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT".The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 BST after they learned of the charges against Thomas.

title: Sex offender bailed to flat near playground
description: Sir Mark said: "Prosecutors rightly opposed bail on multiple occasions, building on officers' clear assessments of the great risk he posed, and yet ba
body: Sir Mark said: "Prosecutors rightly opposed bail on multiple occasions, building on officers' clear assessments of the great risk he posed, and yet bail decisions were ultimately made that prioritised the offender's interests over the safety and the peace of mind of the victims."A victim and their family found themselves living in close proximity to a man who had admitted targeting them."They were so fearful, they ultimately felt forced to move to distant temporary accommodation, disrupting their lives and disrupting their children's lives, simply to escape being in the neighbourhood of the offender."He also criticised "some grossly irresponsible technology and AI companies". He said: "Dogan voyeuristically photographed children known to him before using an AI photo-editing technology to manipulate those images for his own sexual gratification. Companies must do more to prevent their platforms and tools from being used to facilitate sexual offending and harm."Innovation cannot come at the expense of public safety, and industry has a clear responsibility to help prevent these technologies being exploited by predators."Victims, in this case extremely young children and their families, deserve better from both the tech companies and the criminal justice system."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external.
